steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on what technical innovations AI systems need in order to be effectively regulated, and where purely technical work isn't enough. Explain why we use public-sector AI procurement checklists as our lens and lay out how the paper approaches the question.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Regulation protects citizens; push to regulate AI
- Modern AI is hard to regulate; regulatable AI by design
- Our questions
- Lens: public sector AI procurement checklists
- Approach: two checklists, categories, gaps, interdisciplinary aspects
- Assumptions and goal

  - uncheckable requirement = no protection
  - if AI should be regulated, it must be designed to be regulatable
- Questions
  - what innovations in AI systems are needed for effective regulation?
  - where will AI methods alone be insufficient, needing interdisciplinary approaches?
- Lens: procurement checklists
  - pragmatic perspective on regulatable AI broadly

  - intersection of policy-making and practical implementation
  - desiderata comprehensive, reflected in nascent private sector regulation efforts (cite)
  - among the more developed AI regulations, several rounds of refinement (cite)
  - focus is to make discussion concrete; innovations relevant to wider discourse
- Approach
  - two checklists: WEF AI Procurement in a Box (cite), Canadian Directive on Automated Decision-Making, CDADM (cite)
  - Figure 1: group technical criteria into categories: (pre-training) data checks, (post-hoc) system monitoring, global explanation, local explanation, objective design, privacy, human + AI systems
  - per category: summarize existing technical approaches
  - identify where more innovation needed to vet complex AI in varied contexts
  - example: large language models hard to evaluate (open-ended nature, data leakage); HELM (cite), Elo ratings (cite) proposed; still unresolved

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Regulations are a basic mechanism that governments use to fulfill their duty of protecting citizens from different threats, including health risks, financial fraud, and discriminatory practices. AI systems are getting more advanced and more integrated into our lives, and so there is more urgency to make sure they align with social values and norms and that their benefits are much bigger than any potential harm. Because of this, legal and regulatory bodies around the world are working hard to develop comprehensive AI regulations.

But present-day AI systems are getting larger, more general, more opaque, and more closed, and this makes effective regulation very challenging. Even if requirements can be written down, it is not clear if and how we can verify that an AI system follows them. If a requirement can't be checked, it won't really protect anyone. So if we think AI systems should be regulated, AI systems have to be designed to be regulatable.

In this article we look at these questions: What innovations in AI systems do we need so that they can be regulated effectively? And in which areas are innovations in AI methods alone not enough, so that more interdisciplinary approaches are needed?

- Lens: procurement checklists
  - pragmatic perspective; codify regulatory requirements for public sector AI adoption; intersection of policy-making and practical implementation
  - desiderata comprehensive, reflected in nascent private sector efforts; among more developed AI regulations, several rounds of refinement
  - focus makes discussion concrete; innovations relevant to wider discourse
- Approach
  - WEF AI Procurement in a Box, Canadian Directive on Automated Decision-Making (CDADM)
  - Figure 1 categories: (pre-training) data checks, (post-hoc) system monitoring, global explanation, local explanation, objective design, privacy, human + AI systems
  - existing approaches per category; where more innovation needed
  - LLM evaluation example: open-ended nature, data leakage; HELM, Elo ratings; still unresolved
  - aspects that seem technical but need interdisciplinary approaches
- Assumptions and goal
  - enough qualified AI + domain experts
  - how far experts can vet now; (non-comprehensive, concrete) list of directions
  - verified against checklists -> progress toward regulatable AI

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Regulations are a basic mechanism that governments use to fulfill their duty of protecting citizens from different threats, including health risks, financial fraud, and discriminatory practices. AI systems are getting more advanced and more integrated into our lives, and so there is more urgency to make sure they align with social values and norms and that their benefits are much bigger than any potential harm. Because of this, legal and regulatory bodies around the world are working hard to develop comprehensive AI regulations.

But present-day AI systems are getting larger, more general, more opaque, and more closed, and this makes effective regulation very challenging. Even if requirements can be written down, it is not clear if and how we can verify that an AI system follows them. If a requirement can't be checked, it won't really protect anyone. So if we think AI systems should be regulated, AI systems have to be designed to be regulatable.

In this article we look at these questions: What innovations in AI systems do we need so that they can be regulated effectively? And in which areas are innovations in AI methods alone not enough, so that more interdisciplinary approaches are needed?

We look at the answer through public sector AI procurement checklists, which give a pragmatic perspective on the bigger challenges of regulatable AI systems. These checklists are not only criteria for government procurement. They are also efforts to codify regulatory requirements for adopting AI systems in the public sector, which puts them at the intersection of policy-making and practical implementation. The desiderata in these checklists are comprehensive, and they show up in the still nascent efforts to regulate AI in the private sector. Also, public sector procurement checklists are some of the more developed AI regulations, and some have gone through several rounds of refinement. We focus on public sector procurement checklists to make the discussion concrete, but the technical innovations needed to satisfy them are relevant to the wider discussion of creating regulatable AI systems.

In particular we look closely at the technical criteria from two existing procurement checklists, the World Economic Forum's AI Procurement in a Box (WEF) and the Canadian Directive on Automated Decision-Making (CDADM). First we group the technical criteria in these two checklists into categories that AI researchers and engineers will know, as shown in Figure 1: (pre-training) data checks, (post-hoc) system monitoring, global explanation, local explanation, objective design, privacy, and human + AI systems. For each category we briefly summarize the existing technical approaches that could be used to build AI systems that meet the criteria. Then we identify areas where relevant technical approaches might exist, but more technical innovation is needed to vet AI systems that are more and more complex and used in more and more varied contexts. For example, large language models are spreading, and they are very hard to evaluate because of things like their open-ended nature and data leakage. Innovative approaches like Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) and Elo ratings have been proposed, but evaluating these models accurately is still an unresolved issue, and more technical advances are needed for effective regulation and oversight. Last, we briefly outline the aspects of these criteria that seem technical but actually need interdisciplinary approaches to vet.

In this whole exercise we assume there are no concerns about expertise, meaning that there are enough qualified AI and domain experts to review if the AI system meets the checklist criteria. What we care about is identifying how far experts can currently vet AI systems against these criteria, and giving a list (not comprehensive, but concrete) of directions for technical innovation to close the gap towards regulatable AI systems. If AI systems can be verified against these checklists, we will have made a lot of progress towards creating regulatable AI systems in general.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Regulations are a fundamental mechanism through which governments fulfill their duty to protect citizens from a variety of threats, including health risks, financial fraud, and discriminatory practices. As AI systems become more advanced and integrated into our lives, there is a corresponding urgency to ensure that they align with social values and norms and that their benefits significantly outweigh any potential harm. In response, legal and regulatory bodies around the world are making a concerted effort to develop comprehensive AI regulations [1,2,3].

However, the increasing size, generality, opaqueness, and closed nature of present-day AI systems pose significant challenges to effective regulation [4,5]. Even when requirements can be articulated, it remains unclear whether and how we can verify an AI system's adherence to them. A requirement that cannot be checked will not provide effective protection. If we believe that AI systems should be regulated, then AI systems must be designed to be regulatable.

In this article, we consider the following questions: What innovations in AI systems are needed for them to be effectively regulated? And in what areas will innovations in AI methods alone be insufficient, so that more interdisciplinary approaches are required?

We explore the answer through the lens of public sector AI procurement checklists, which offer a pragmatic perspective on the broader challenges of regulatable AI systems. These checklists do more than outline criteria for government procurement; they are concerted efforts to codify regulatory requirements for the adoption of AI systems in the public sector, which places them at the intersection of policy-making and practical implementation. The desiderata in these checklists are comprehensive and are reflected in still nascent efforts to regulate AI in the private sector [2,6]. Moreover, public sector procurement checklists are among the more developed AI regulations, and some have gone through several rounds of refinement [7]. We focus on public sector procurement checklists to make our discussion concrete; the technical innovations needed to satisfy them are relevant to the wider discourse on creating regulatable AI systems.

Specifically, we closely examine the technical criteria from two existing procurement checklists: the World Economic Forum's AI Procurement in a Box (WEF) [8] and the Canadian Directive on Automated Decision-Making (CDADM) [9]. As shown in Figure 1, we first group the technical criteria in these two checklists into categories familiar to AI researchers and engineers: (pre-training) data checks, (post-hoc) system monitoring, global explanation, local explanation, objective design, privacy, and human + AI systems. For each category, we briefly summarize existing technical approaches that could be used to build AI systems meeting those criteria. Next, we identify areas where relevant technical approaches may exist but additional technical innovation is needed to vet increasingly complex AI systems used in increasingly varied contexts. For example, the proliferation of large language models brings significant difficulty in evaluation, due to factors such as their open-ended nature and data leakage. Although innovative approaches like Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) [10] and Elo ratings [11] have been proposed, accurately evaluating these models remains an unresolved issue that requires further technical advances for effective regulation and oversight. Finally, we briefly outline aspects of these criteria that may seem technical but in fact require interdisciplinary approaches to vet.

Throughout this exercise, we assume no concerns about expertise; that is, we assume there are enough qualified AI and domain experts to review whether the AI system meets the checklist criteria. Our concern is to identify to what extent experts can currently vet AI systems against these criteria, and to provide a (non-comprehensive, but concrete) list of directions for technical innovation to bridge the gap towards regulatable AI systems. If AI systems can be verified against these checklists, we will have made significant progress towards creating regulatable AI systems in general.
